bible_refs.note: Ἰδοὺ τίθημι ἐν Σιὼν λίθον ἀκρογωνιαῖον, ἐκλεκτόν, ἔντιμον, καὶ ὁ πιστεύων ἐπ' αὐτῷ
λίθος ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες, οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας
Ἰδοὺ οὗτος κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ
«Καὶ σοῦ δὲ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται ῥομφαία, ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν διαλογισμοί» matches Luke 2:35 exactly in the Septuagint tradition.

The reference to Cleopatras (Cleopas) on the way to Emmaus, where Christ meets him and explains the scriptures, alludes to Luke 24:13-32, though the name is Hellenized and the dialogue is paraphrased.
The mention of Mary Magdalene's weak reasoning alludes to her state at the tomb in John 20:11-18, where she does not at first recognize the risen Christ.

choices.why: The noun ἀνάστασις in this context refers to spiritual or bodily raising up, not merely 'resurrection' as a technical term, matching the parallel with falling (πτῶσιν).
The compound ἀκρογωνιαῖον λίθον is a technical architectural term for the foundational corner stone, best rendered as 'cornerstone' in English theological usage.

choices.english: the one who believes on him
choices.why: The articular present participle ὁ πιστεύων with ἐπ' indicates ongoing trust, best rendered as 'the one who believes on him' to preserve the grammatical nuance.

choices.english: A sword shall pierce your own soul
choices.why: The phrase uses a genitive of possession (σοῦ τὴν ψυχήν) meaning 'your soul'; ῥομφαία is a large sword or dagger, often used metaphorically for piercing grief; the future indicative διαλεύσεται indicates a piercing action, so 'shall pierce' conveys both futurity and penetration.
rejected: your soul will go through a sword

choices.term: Ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν διαλογισμοί
choices.english: so that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare
choices.why: The clause uses ἵνα with subjunctive ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν for purpose; ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν means 'out of many hearts' (source of the thoughts); διαλογισμοί here means inner thoughts or reasonings, not just 'thoughts' abstractly; ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν is passive aorist subjunctive, best rendered 'may be revealed' or 'may be laid bare' to convey uncovering.
rejected: so that from many hearts thoughts may be revealed
that the reasonings of many hearts might become known

choices.why: χωρὶς + genitive (φθορᾶς) means 'without'; τεχθέντα is the perfect passive participle of τίκτω, 'to beget, bear', here referring to the eternal generation of the Word; the phrase is a theological term of art from Nicene Christology, so 'begotten without corruption' is the standard rendering in patristic English for this precise formulation.

χωρὶς ἀνδρὸς is a literal 'without man', but in context of virgin birth, it refers to conception without human father; συλληφθέντα is aorist passive participle of συλλαμβάνω, 'to seize, take, conceive'; while 'conceived without man' is more idiomatic, the author's phrasing emphasizes the seizure or taking of the body in a way that bypasses natural generation, so 'seized without man' preserves the stark, almost violent patristic language of the incarnation as a divine intrusion.

choices.english: who did not open the womb
choices.why: οὐκ ἀνοίξαντα is aorist active participle of ἀνοίγω, 'to open'; τὴν μῆτραν is 'the womb'; this refers to the doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity, specifically that she did not suffer the usual opening of the womb in parturition; the literal phrasing is theologically precise and must be retained as is, not paraphrased as 'remained a virgin' which adds conceptual content not in the Greek.
rejected: who did not break the seal of her womb

pass_b_english: He spoke of the rising of many in Israel. This was concerning whom Peter, having taken up Isaiah’s prophecy, sent to the churches. ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone, a cornerstone, elect and honored, and whoever believes on him shall not be put to shame.’ Then he added the prophecy, interpreting it in agreement with Simeon as he spoke: ‘To you, therefore, belongs honor if you believe; but the unbelievers reject the stone which the builders threw away—this very stone has become the head of the corner, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. Those who stumble over it do so because they disobey the word.’ Therefore, it was not laid for the fall of the unbelievers and the rising of the faithful. For those who thought they stood by the law cast themselves down by their unbelief. But these others, amid the multitude of their sins and existing among the fallen, rushed to the staff of faith and raised themselves up.

‘Behold, this one lies for the fall and rising of many in Israel and for a sign that is contradicted.’ What is this? It is the cross. For this sign, after being filled with sufferings and wonders, was contradicted. He was naked, and he hid the sun; he fastened the nails and shook the stones; he opened his side with a spear and opened the tombs of the dead. From this, the sign became one that is contradicted. The unbelievers indeed left these things and looked away, but the faithful, after the sufferings, beheld the wonders. Thus, at that time, the crowd of the Pharisees wandered about him, but the centurion declared him to be the Son of God, and having spoken, he worshipped.
To these things belong the following corresponding matters.
And a sword shall pierce your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare.
This sword is the discernment that will pass through your soul according to the time of the cross.
For you will marvel to see upon the cross him who was begotten without corruption, seized without man, who did not open the womb and whose own birth acted impassibly and incorruptibly.
What then will come to pass from here? 'So that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare.'

Perhaps indeed this will happen among others, but much more surely among those who had been disciples of the Lord, who had beheld his sufferings and the deeds he performed, and who had endured the winter of reasonings from both sides— for example, Cleopas, who suffered from the things that the Christ, upon meeting him on the way to Emmaus, revealed to him.

For when Cleopas was asked why he was sad and his heart was confused, he spoke little about Christ and what the time allowed, not knowing to whom he was speaking; having spoken, he added: 'We had hoped that he was the one about to redeem Israel'— that is, our hope had become foreign to him and had gone out.
And the reasoning of Mary Magdalene was also revealed, being weak.
This happened of the Christ having been crucified.
